chapter_title: A Tale of Three Intersecting Lines

zero_omission_notes.summary: This chapter explores triangles formed by three pairwise intersecting lines. It establishes the Triangle Inequality Theorem, conditions for triangle existence, and triangle classification by side lengths (Equilateral, Isosceles, Scalene).

detailed_sections.full_notes: Three lines intersecting pairwise at three distinct points form a triangle.

margin_notes_and_sidebars.title: Straight vs Roundabout
margin_notes_and_sidebars.content: The direct line between two points is always shorter than a detour through a third point.

detailed_sections.full_notes: A triangle exists if and only if the sum of any two side lengths is strictly greater than the third side: a + b > c, b + c > a, c + a > b. Practical test: Sum of two smallest sides > longest side.
1. Equilateral: a = b = c. 2. Isosceles: two sides equal. 3. Scalene: all sides unequal.

margin_notes_and_sidebars.title: Equilateral Feasibility
margin_notes_and_sidebars.content: For any side length s > 0, s + s = 2s > s is always true.

practical_lab_activity_or_methodology_ma.aim_or_objective: Test triangle construction using ruler and compass for various side combinations
procedure_or_steps: Draw arc of radius a from one end.
Draw arc of radius b from other end.
practical_lab_activity_or_methodology_ma.observations_or_results: Arcs intersect only if a + b > c. If a + b <= c, arcs never cross.
practical_lab_activity_or_methodology_ma.conclusion_or_principle: Triangles exist iff the sum of any two side lengths exceeds the third side.

Triangle with three distinct side lengths

textbook_exercises.question: Can 24, 26, 28 form a triangle?
textbook_exercises.answer: Yes. Smallest sides sum = 24 + 26 = 50 > 28. Thus a triangle exists.

objective_questions_1_mark.question: Which side set can form a triangle?

short_answer_questions.question: Two sides of a triangle measure 6 cm and 10 cm. Find the range of the third side x.
short_answer_questions.answer: Upper bound: x < 6 + 10 => x < 16. Lower bound: x + 6 > 10 => x > 4. Range: 4 cm < x < 16 cm.

analytical_reasoning_questions.question: Explain why a triangle cannot have side lengths 3 cm, 6 cm, 9 cm.
analytical_reasoning_questions.answer: Sum of two smaller sides = 3 + 6 = 9 cm. The longest side = 9 cm. Since 9 is not strictly greater than 9 (9 = 9), the two sides lie flat along the 9 cm segment, forming no triangle.

competency_and_case_studies.case_scenario: A surveyor maps roads AB = 12 km, BC = 20 km, AC = 40 km.

qa.question: Can towns A, B, C form a triangle?
qa.answer: AB + BC = 12 + 20 = 32 km < 40 km. They cannot form a triangle.

common_misconceptions_and_pitfalls.common_error_or_misconception: Checking only one arbitrary pair of sides instead of the two smallest sides.
common_misconceptions_and_pitfalls.correct_fact_or_method: Always test whether the sum of the two smallest sides strictly exceeds the longest side.
